Christian Foundational Holidays Power North America's Retail Boom – Losing This Heritage Risks major damage to Social and Business Structures, 

Business/Society - December 31, 2025

As retailers tally another record-breaking holiday season, the enduring impact of holidays with Christian roots—and those tied to Christian observances—remains the cornerstone of North America's retail landscape. We are a multicultural society, not multi-religious in our public celebrations; enriched by immigrants from every corner of the globe who bring diverse ethnic traditions, foods, languages, and customs, yet share a common cultural calendar largely shaped by Christian foundational holidays.

Canada's culture, laws, statutory holidays, and public observances are historically rooted in Christian foundations. From the British North America Act and the enduring influence of common law shaped by Christian ethics, to statutory holidays such as Christmas, Good Friday, and Easter Monday, the nation's official calendar and workplace structure reflect this heritage. Community events, school breaks, retail promotions, performing arts seasons, and even food traditions (from Christmas turkey dinners to Easter chocolate) are built upon this framework. This shared structure provides the rhythm for economic and social life, enabling predictable seasonal surges that businesses, arts organizations, and service industries depend on for planning and profitability.

This shared calendar has attempted to be influenced by shifting immigration patterns. Two decades ago, in the early 2000s, Canada's top immigrant source countries included significant numbers from Europe (e.g., UK), the Philippines (predominantly Christian), and China (many with Christian or no religious affiliation), resulting in many newcomers being of Christian background or no faith. In contrast, recent years have seen India as the dominant source country, with growing numbers from other South Asian and Middle Eastern nations, leading to a higher proportion of immigrants affiliated with Sikhism, Hinduism, and Islam.

In this society, Christmas leads as the retail powerhouse, supplemented by Easter, the eve of All Saints' Day (commonly known as Halloween), Saint Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, and Father's Day—each blending historical Christian connections with cultural evolutions that have been embraced across ethnic backgrounds.

These Christian-foundational holidays form the seasonal backbone that drives the shopping traditions millions of North Americans enjoy today, regardless of personal belief. The widespread participation reflects how holidays originating in Christian traditions—celebrating events like the birth and resurrection of Christ, honoring saints, and family values inspired by Christian teachings—have become shared cultural milestones, adapted with ethnic flavors and enjoyed by people of various cultural heritages in a pluralistic, yet culturally unified society.

The surge in holiday advertising tied to these observances is also critical to the survival of media across all genres. From television and radio to newspapers, magazines, digital platforms, podcasts, and streaming services, the November-December period alone often generates 30-50% or more of annual advertising revenue for many outlets. Retailers’ massive holiday campaigns—featuring Christmas sales, gift guides, and festive promotions—provide the financial oxygen that keeps newsrooms staffed, entertainment programming funded, local radio stations on air, and independent digital publishers viable. A decline in these Christian-foundational holiday traditions would slash this vital ad revenue, triggering layoffs, reduced content quality, station closures, and the potential collapse of free or low-cost media that informs and entertains the public year-round.

If these Christian observances and holidays were to fade or be deliberately eroded from our public life, the consequences would be devastating. The sudden or gradual disappearance of the Christmas surge—accounting for nearly one-fifth of annual retail revenue—could unleash a devastating economic tsunami: iconic department stores shuttering, toy empires crumbling, jewelry and apparel chains collapsing under unsustainable debt, and entire supply chains grinding to a halt. Tens of thousands of seasonal and permanent jobs could vanish, leaving families destitute and communities hollowed out. In the performing arts, the lifeblood of holiday productions would dry up—The Nutcracker stages going dark, A Christmas Carol theaters boarding up windows, beloved Messiah sing-alongs silenced forever—forcing orchestras, ballet companies, and regional playhouses into bankruptcy, mass layoffs, and permanent closure. This cultural void would rip away generational traditions, fracture community bonds, and leave a sterile, unpredictable calendar that no alternative celebrations could adequately replace—triggering a profound crisis in both economic stability and national identity.

Holiday performing arts events, such as Christmas concerts, ballets like The Nutcracker, and theatrical productions including A Christmas Carol, represent a significant portion of seasonal arts revenue. These performances often account for 40-50% or more of annual ticket sales for many ballet companies and theaters, serving as financial lifelines amid rising costs. Audiences for these holiday shows are predominantly drawn from those who culturally or religiously connect with the Christian themes, with families and communities treating them as cherished traditions. While some individuals from non-Christian backgrounds may attend secular or community versions, mainstream religious or themed Christmas concerts and plays see primary attendance from Christian-identifying or culturally Christian audiences, driving the bulk of this revenue stream.

Industry experts increasingly advise retailers to embrace specific holiday names like “Christmas” and “Easter” in advertising rather than generic phrases such as “Happy Holidays.” Research and sales data consistently show that consumers—particularly the majority who celebrate these specific traditions—respond more positively to authentic, direct messaging that reflects the actual occasion. Using “Christmas” evokes stronger emotional connections, higher engagement, and better conversion rates in campaigns, as it aligns with how most shoppers think about and plan their spending. Generic terms, while intended to be inclusive, can dilute brand resonance and perceived sincerity, potentially reducing the urgency and excitement that drive seasonal purchases. Major chains that have tested targeted “Merry Christmas” and “Happy Easter” promotions often report uplifts in traffic and sales compared to neutral alternatives, reinforcing that specificity sells when the holidays themselves are culturally specific.

Recent polls highlight this preference in Canada, where a growing majority—around 67%-70%—favor "Merry Christmas" as their holiday greeting, up from previous years, while only 18-24% prefer "Happy Holidays." This public sentiment contrasts with some Liberal politicians who have emphasized "Happy Holidays" in official communications for inclusivity, though the Liberal Party itself has recently used "Merry Christmas" in greetings, drawing mixed reactions. Critics argue that an over-reliance on neutral phrasing by political figures may not fully align with the preferences of most Canadians, potentially influencing how retailers approach their own inclusive yet targeted marketing strategies.

These observances collectively account for a substantial portion of annual retail sales. The winter holiday season (November-December, primarily Christmas-driven) alone represents approximately 18-20% of yearly U.S. retail sales (per NRF and historical Census data). Adding the other major events—Easter (0.4-0.5%), Halloween (0.2-0.3%), Valentine's Day (0.5%), Mother's Day (0.6-0.7%), and Father's Day (~0.4-0.5%)—pushes the combined contribution from these holidays to an estimated 20-25% of total annual retail revenue, depending on the year and categories measured. This underscores their outsized role in driving consumer spending spikes.

These observances are not just cultural touchstones; they are essential lifelines for the retail industry. When combined with the boosts from Easter ($24 billion), Halloween ($13 billion), Valentine's Day ($28 billion), Mother's Day ($34 billion), and Father's Day (~$24 billion), these holidays contribute hundreds of billions in additional revenue, providing critical momentum across the calendar.

Retailers rely heavily on these Christian-foundational holidays and observances for survival and growth. A poor performance in just the November-December period can push marginal chains into distress, while consistent weakness across multiple seasons exacerbates vulnerabilities. Industry experts note that without these seasonal surges—particularly the massive Christmas lift—many retailers, especially in seasonal, gift, and apparel categories, would face severe financial strain or closure. Historical patterns show that failed holiday seasons have contributed to waves of bankruptcies, as seen in past downturns where weak consumer spending led to store closings and insolvencies. Hypothetically, if these observances disappeared entirely, a substantial portion of the sector could collapse, with toy stores, department stores, and specialty retailers hit hardest—potentially forcing thousands of locations to shutter and reshaping the retail landscape dramatically.

The Christmas season delivered once more. In the United States, Visa and Mastercard data showed November-December spending up ~4% year-over-year, approaching the National Retail Federation's (NRF) forecasted $1 trillion+ milestone.

Canada saw a similar 4.4% rise per Visa, with strong clothing and care categories, and per-person gift intentions around $975 CAD.

Easter (resurrection of Christ) contributed ~$23.6 billion in U.S. spending (2025 NRF), driven by food, candy, gifts, and apparel. Canadian celebrations emphasized family and spring items.

Halloween (October 31), the vigil before All Saints' Day—a Christian feast honoring saints—has grown into a major fall retail event with ancient Celtic influences but strong ties to the Christian calendar through All Hallows' Eve. In 2025, U.S. consumers spent a record $13.1 billion (per NRF), including $3.9 billion on candy, $4.3 billion on costumes, and $4.2 billion on decorations. In Canada, while no official aggregate figure is available, Halloween has emerged as one of the fastest-growing retail moments, with many households spending $50-100 on candy, costumes, and décor amid rising participation in trick-or-treating and home decorating.

Saint Valentine's Day, rooted in the Christian feast of martyr Saint Valentine (5th-century liturgy by Pope Gelasius I), generated a record $27.5 billion in the U.S. ($188-189 per person) on candy, outings, flowers, and jewelry. Canadian participation (37%) focused on similar value-driven gifts.

Mother's Day (second Sunday in May) honors motherhood with ties to ancient festivals and Europe's Christian Mothering Sunday (honoring the Virgin Mary during Lent). Its modern North American form was created by Anna Jarvis in 1908–1914 as a personal tribute to her activist mother. In 2025, U.S. spending hit $34.1 billion (84% participation, ~$259 average) on jewelry, experiences, and flowers. Canada mirrors this with robust retail and dining boosts.

Father's Day (third Sunday in June), the complementary counterpart to Mother's Day, originated in the United States in 1910. It was first proposed by Sonora Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington, who wanted to honor her father, Civil War veteran William Jackson Smart—a single parent who raised six children. The first celebration took place on June 19, 1910, at the Spokane YMCA. After years of advocacy, President Lyndon B. Johnson issued a proclamation in 1966, and President Richard Nixon made it a permanent national holiday in 1972. In 2025, U.S. spending reached a record $24 billion, focused on tools, electronics, outings, greeting cards, and apparel—providing a mid-year retail surge.

These occasions, from direct Christian origins to inspired family traditions, create consistent retail waves.

Globally, observance of these holidays varies sharply. Valentine's Day and Halloween face strong opposition in many Muslim-majority countries. Both are widely viewed as incompatible with Islamic teachings due to perceived Christian or pagan roots—Valentine's Day for its romantic and saint-related origins, and Halloween for its ties to ancient Celtic pagan festivals (Samhain), themes of spirits, witchcraft, and the occult. Scholarly consensus often deems participation haram, citing risks of shirk (polytheism), superstition, and imitation of non-Muslims. Countries like Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Pakistan discourage or restrict public celebrations, with limited events confined to expat or tourist areas in places like Dubai or Istanbul.

As post-holiday sales continue, North America's blend of faith, family, and commerce underscores trillions in annual spending from these timeless traditions.

Retailers’ massive holiday campaigns—featuring Christmas sales, gift guides, and festive promotions—provide the financial oxygen that keeps newsrooms staffed, entertainment programming funded, local radio stations on air, and independent digital publishers viable. A decline in these Christian-foundational holiday traditions would slash this vital ad revenue, triggering layoffs, reduced content quality, station closures, and the potential collapse of free or low-cost media that informs and entertains the public year-round. If these Christian observances and holidays were to fade or be deliberately eroded from our public life, the consequences would be devastating. The sudden or gradual disappearance of the Christmas surge—accounting for nearly one-fifth of annual retail revenue—could unleash a devastating economic tsunami: iconic department stores shuttering, toy empires crumbling, jewelry and apparel chains collapsing under unsustainable debt, and entire supply chains grinding to a halt. Tens of thousands of seasonal and permanent jobs could vanish, leaving families destitute and communities hollowed out. In the performing arts, the lifeblood of holiday productions would dry up—The Nutcracker stages going dark, A Christmas Carol theaters boarding up windows, beloved Messiah sing-alongs silenced forever—forcing orchestras, ballet companies, and regional playhouses into bankruptcy, mass layoffs, and permanent closure. This cultural void would rip away generational traditions, fracture community bonds, and leave a sterile, unpredictable calendar that no alternative celebrations could adequately replace—triggering a profound crisis in both economic stability and national identity. Holiday performing arts events, such as Christmas concerts, ballets like The Nutcracker, and theatrical productions including A Christmas Carol, represent a significant portion of seasonal arts revenue. These performances often account for 40-50% or more of annual ticket sales for many ballet companies and theaters, serving as financial lifelines amid rising costs. Audiences for these holiday shows are predominantly drawn from those who culturally or religiously connect with the Christian themes, with families and communities treating them as cherished traditions. While some individuals from non-Christian backgrounds may attend secular or community versions, mainstream religious or themed Christmas concerts and plays see primary attendance from Christian-identifying or culturally Christian audiences, driving the bulk of this revenue stream. Industry experts increasingly advise retailers to embrace specific holiday names like “Christmas” and “Easter” in advertising rather than generic phrases such as “Happy Holidays.” Research and sales data consistently show that consumers—particularly the majority who celebrate these specific traditions—respond more positively to authentic, direct messaging that reflects the actual occasion. Using “Christmas” evokes stronger emotional connections, higher engagement, and better conversion rates in campaigns, as it aligns with how most shoppers think about and plan their spending. Generic terms, while intended to be inclusive, can dilute brand resonance and perceived sincerity, potentially reducing the urgency and excitement that drive seasonal purchases. Major chains that have tested targeted “Merry Christmas” and “Happy Easter” promotions often report uplifts in traffic and sales compared to neutral alternatives, reinforcing that specificity sells when the holidays themselves are culturally specific. Recent polls highlight this preference in Canada, where a growing majority—around 67%-70%—favor "Merry Christmas" as their holiday greeting, up from previous years, while only 18-24% prefer "Happy Holidays." This public sentiment contrasts with some Liberal politicians who have emphasized "Happy Holidays" in official communications for inclusivity, though the Liberal Party itself has recently used "Merry Christmas" in greetings, drawing mixed reactions. Critics argue that an over-reliance on neutral phrasing by political figures may not fully align with the preferences of most Canadians, potentially influencing how retailers approach their own inclusive yet targeted marketing strategies. These observances collectively account for a substantial portion of annual retail sales. The winter holiday season (November-December, primarily Christmas-driven) alone represents approximately 18-20% of yearly U.S. retail sales (per NRF and historical Census data). Adding the other major events—Easter (0.4-0.5%), Halloween (0.2-0.3%), Valentine's Day (0.5%), Mother's Day (0.6-0.7%), and Father's Day (~0.4-0.5%)—pushes the combined contribution from these holidays to an estimated 20-25% of total annual retail revenue, depending on the year and categories measured. This underscores their outsized role in driving consumer spending spikes. These observances are not just cultural touchstones; they are essential lifelines for the retail industry. When combined with the boosts from Easter ($24 billion), Halloween ($13 billion), Valentine's Day ($28 billion), Mother's Day ($34 billion), and Father's Day (~$24 billion), these holidays contribute hundreds of billions in additional revenue, providing critical momentum across the calendar. Retailers rely heavily on these Christian-foundational holidays and observances for survival and growth. A poor performance in just the November-December period can push marginal chains into distress, while consistent weakness across multiple seasons exacerbates vulnerabilities. Industry experts note that without these seasonal surges—particularly the massive Christmas lift—many retailers, especially in seasonal, gift, and apparel categories, would face severe financial strain or closure. Historical patterns show that failed holiday seasons have contributed to waves of bankruptcies, as seen in past downturns where weak consumer spending led to store closings and insolvencies. Hypothetically, if these observances disappeared entirely, a substantial portion of the sector could collapse, with toy stores, department stores, and specialty retailers hit hardest—potentially forcing thousands of locations to shutter and reshaping the retail landscape dramatically. The Christmas season delivered once more. In the United States, Visa and Mastercard data showed November-December spending up ~4% year-over-year, approaching the National Retail Federation's (NRF) forecasted $1 trillion+ milestone. Canada saw a similar 4.4% rise per Visa, with strong clothing and care categories, and per-person gift intentions around $975 CAD. Easter (resurrection of Christ) contributed ~$23.6 billion in U.S. spending (2025 NRF), driven by food, candy, gifts, and apparel. Canadian celebrations emphasized family and spring items. Halloween (October 31), the vigil before All Saints' Day—a Christian feast honoring saints—has grown into a major fall retail event with ancient Celtic influences but strong ties to the Christian calendar through All Hallows' Eve. In 2025, U.S. consumers spent a record $13.1 billion (per NRF), including $3.9 billion on candy, $4.3 billion on costumes, and $4.2 billion on decorations. In Canada, while no official aggregate figure is available, Halloween has emerged as one of the fastest-growing retail moments, with many households spending $50-100 on candy, costumes, and décor amid rising participation in trick-or-treating and home decorating. Saint Valentine's Day, rooted in the Christian feast of martyr Saint Valentine (5th-century liturgy by Pope Gelasius I), generated a record $27.5 billion in the U.S. ($188-189 per person) on candy, outings, flowers, and jewelry. Canadian participation (37%) focused on similar value-driven gifts. Mother's Day (second Sunday in May) honors motherhood with ties to ancient festivals and Europe's Christian Mothering Sunday (honoring the Virgin Mary during Lent). Its modern North American form was created by Anna Jarvis in 1908–1914 as a personal tribute to her activist mother. In 2025, U.S. spending hit $34.1 billion (84% participation, ~$259 average) on jewelry, experiences, and flowers. Canada mirrors this with robust retail and dining boosts. Father's Day (third Sunday in June), the complementary counterpart to Mother's Day, originated in the United States in 1910. It was first proposed by Sonora Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington, who wanted to honor her father, Civil War veteran William Jackson Smart—a single parent who raised six children. The first celebration took place on June 19, 1910, at the Spokane YMCA. After years of advocacy, President Lyndon B. Johnson issued a proclamation in 1966, and President Richard Nixon made it a permanent national holiday in 1972. In 2025, U.S. spending reached a record $24 billion, focused on tools, electronics, outings, greeting cards, and apparel—providing a mid-year retail surge. These occasions, from direct Christian origins to inspired family traditions, create consistent retail waves. Globally, observance of these holidays varies sharply. Valentine's Day and Halloween face strong opposition in many Muslim-majority countries. Both are widely viewed as incompatible with Islamic teachings due to perceived Christian or pagan roots—Valentine's Day for its romantic and saint-related origins, and Halloween for its ties to ancient Celtic pagan festivals (Samhain), themes of spirits, witchcraft, and the occult. Scholarly consensus often deems participation haram, citing risks of shirk (polytheism), superstition, and imitation of non-Muslims. Countries like Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Pakistan discourage or restrict public celebrations, with limited events confined to expat or tourist areas in places like Dubai or Istanbul. As post-holiday sales continue, North America's blend of faith, family, and commerce underscores trillions in annual spending from these timeless traditions.
